canonicalExplanation.summary: **Normal flow** is how the browser lays out elements with no layout CSS: **block** boxes (div, p, h1, section) stack top to bottom and take the full width; **inline** boxes (a, em, span) sit side by side within lines of text. `display` changes a box's behaviour: `block`, `inline`, `inline-block`, `flex`, `grid`, `none`. Start from a document that reads well in normal flow, then **enhance** the arrangement — don't pull everything out of flow.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A developer positions every card on a page with `position: absolute` and exact pixel offsets. It looks perfect on their laptop — and overlaps into chaos on a phone, at zoom, or when a title gets longer. A document remains readable in source order before grid enhances the card arrangement. In this lesson you'll predict and repair layout using normal flow and appropriate display behaviour. ```predict {"question": "Three `

` elements with no CSS. How are they arranged?", "options": ["Side by side", "Stacked vertically, each full width"], "answer": 1, "why": "p is a block element: in normal flow, blocks stack top to bottom."} ```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Box model, sizing and overflow** module, **Sections and landmarks**, **Content, padding, border and margin**, and **Document tree and DOM concept**.

sections.heading: The model: blocks stack, inlines flow in lines
sections.body:
| display | Behaviour | Typical elements |
|---|---|---|
| `block`. | new line, full available width. | div, p, h1, section. |
| `inline`. | flows in text; width/height ignored. | a, span, em. |
| `inline-block`. | flows in text but accepts width/padding. | buttons in a sentence. |
| `flex` / `grid`. | block outside, new layout for children. | component containers. |
| `none`. | removed from layout and accessibility tree. | hidden content. |

```css
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
/* without this rule, the cards simply stack in source order — still readable */
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why doesn't `width: 200px` work on a span?", "answer": "A span is inline by default; inline boxes ignore width and height. Change it to inline-block (or block) if it needs a size."}
```

sections.heading: Stay in flow

includes: Predict block and inline behaviour in normal flow and choose display values.
Enhance a readable source-order document with grid or flex instead of taking elements out of flow.

outcomes: Predict and repair layout using normal flow and appropriate display behavior.

examples.title: Readable first, arranged second
examples.situation: A document remains readable in source order before grid enhances the card arrangement.
walkthrough: **Normal flow first:** with no layout CSS, the heading, intro and six course cards stack in source order — fully readable.
**Enhance:** `.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr)); }` arranges cards in columns when space allows.
**Check:** at 320px the browser will render one column, at 1200px three — and the reading order never changes.
examples.result: The page reads correctly with or without the grid, and the layout adapts to any width.

examples.title: The absolutely positioned page
examples.situation: Cards use `position: absolute; top: 120px; left: 340px;` etc. A longer title in card 2 overlaps card 5.
walkthrough: Absolute boxes are removed from flow, so they don't push each other.
Any change in content or screen size causes overlap.
Fix: remove the absolute positions and use grid with gaps; content now reflows.
examples.result: Cards never overlap, whatever their content length.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Modern layouts should remove every element from normal flow for precise control.
misconceptions.correction: Normal flow automatically handles content length, zoom and screen size. Layouts should start from a readable flow and enhance it with flex or grid; taking elements out of flow should be the exception.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The absolutely positioned page", why did the cards overlap?

analogy.example: Normal flow is like **text in a book**: paragraphs stack, words wrap onto new lines. Grid is like arranging the book's pages on a table in rows. Absolute positioning is like gluing each paragraph to a fixed spot — fine until the text changes.
limitations: Books don't resize; web pages do constantly.
display:none is like tearing a page out — nobody can read it.

steps.explanation: The document remains readable in source order.
Grid then enhances the card arrangement into columns.
The same source adapts without breaking its order.

trace.textAlternative: Enhancing normal flow with grid. Step 1, Normal flow: order is h1, p, cards; layout is stacked. The document remains readable in source order. Step 2, Enhance: cards is grid columns. Grid then enhances the card arrangement into columns. Step 3, Adapt: 320px is 1 column; 1200px is 3 columns; reading order is unchanged. The same source adapts without breaking its order.

remediation.explanation: Delete your layout CSS temporarily. Does the page still read in a sensible order? If not, fix the HTML order first. Then add flex or grid back.

recap.summary: To predict and repair layout using normal flow, remember blocks stack and inlines flow in lines, choose display values deliberately, keep a readable source order, and enhance it with flex or grid rather than removing elements from flow.
